doc.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 23, 2003 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Jazz too angry; avoiding social messages and free jazz
summary: Bucky thinks jazz should be happy, disliked free jazz, and prefers playing standards like Honeysuckle Rose.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Would you say that jazz has become a little too angry these days?
Is there a reason for that?

I don’t know. I don’t know. It might be the guys who are putting it out. There’s no room for that. Jazz is supposed to be happy. If you want to send a social message, do something else. But don’t take it out on music.
Don’t take it out on music.
That’s right. Because you’re supposed to get the people going, they’ve got to like the melody and they’ve got to like what you’re doing, and you’re going in the wrong
direction when you start making speeches with music, on a soapbox. There’s no room for that in my—
Well do you recall hearing things like “Ascension” and “Free Jazz,” Ornette Coleman, those kinds of things in the 60s?

I heard it, yes, but I didn’t like it. And what can I do about it? I can still play “Honeysuckle Rose” you know, and make everybody happy. Or it makes me happy. And I’ve been playing it all my life since I was ten years old. And who says you can’t do it over and over again? You know Zoot Sims played seven or eight tunes that he was known for. And it was better each time, each time. And he’d play tunes he didn’t know and it always came out great. And Benny Goodman, look how many records Benny made.

You don’t hear Benny putting everything in the ground you know. And when you hear those old bands playing, they’re playing with a little pepper, zip, you know, boom, boom, boom, boom. They’re playing the hard stuff. Listen to the brass section behind Frank Sinatra. They’re blowing their hearts out for forty-one and a quarter.
